'''''Epilobium ciliatum''''', known by the common names '''fringed willowherb''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=EPCI|taxon=Epilobium ciliatum|accessdate=27 June 2016}}</ref> '''American willowherb''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |accessdate=27 June 2016 }}</ref> '''slender willow herb''', and '''northern willow herb''' is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the willowherb family [[Onagraceae]]. This species is native to much of [[North America]], southern [[South America]], and [[East Asia]]. It is an [[introduced species]] in much of Eurasia and Australia.<ref name="jepson">{{cite web |url=http://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/cgi-bin/get_JM_treatment.pl?5263,5410,5417 | title=Jepson Flora Project:Onagraceae |accessdate=18 July 2013}}</ref>

This [[perennial]] [[herbaceous plant]] usually occurs in wetlands, but may be found in a great variety of habitats, including disturbed areas and roadsides, at elevations below {{convert|1400|m|ft}}.<ref name="jepson"/>

==Description==
''Epilobium ciliatum'' is a clumping perennial often exceeding {{convert|1.5|m|ft|sigfig=1}} in height. It has thickly veined lance-shaped leaves which may be up to 15 centimeters long toward the base of the plant. The foliage, stem, and [[inflorescence]] are covered in bristly hairs and glands.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Northern Willow Herb, Epilobium ciliatum|url=https://calscape.org/Epilobium-ciliatum-()|access-date=|website=calscape.org}}</ref>

There are four sepals. The regular, trumpet-shaped flowers have four petals which are so deeply notched they look like four pairs. They are white to light purple or pink with dark veining.<ref name=":0" /> There are eight stamens and a club-shaped stigma. The fruit is a narrow, hairy, four-chambered capsule up to 10 centimeters in length which may be held on a long stalk. The seeds are downy and can float for long distances with the wind.<ref name=NatureGate>{{cite web |url=http://www.luontoportti.com/suomi/en/kukkakasvit/american-willowherb |title=American Willowherb |publisher=NatureGate |accessdate=2013-12-24}}</ref>

* ''Epilobium ciliatum'' ssp. ''glandulosum'' — <small>(Lehm.) Hoch & P.H.Raven</small> <ref>[http://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/cgi-bin/get_JM_treatment.pl?5263,5410,5417,5419 Jepson: ''Epilobium ciliatum'' ssp. ''glandulosum'']</ref><ref>[https://plants.usda.gov/java/profile?symbol=EPCIG USDA: ''Epilobium ciliatum'' ssp. ''glandulosum'']</ref>
* ''Epilobium ciliatum'' ssp. ''watsonii'' — <small>(Barbey) Hoch & P.H.Raven</small><ref>[http://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/cgi-bin/get_JM_treatment.pl?5263,5410,5417,5420 Jepson: ''Epilobium ciliatum'' ssp. ''watsonii'']</ref><ref>[https://plants.usda.gov/java/profile?symbol=EPCIW USDA:''Epilobium ciliatum'' ssp. ''watsonii'']</ref>

===Taxonomy===
''Epilobium ciliatum'' may be a [[cryptic species complex]]. The Rocky Mountain Willowherb (''Epilobium saximontanum'') is sometimes included as yet another subspecies.

The three currently recognized subspecies may each constitute a distinct species. If so, ''E. ciliatum'' ssp. ''watsonii'' would perhaps use the name ''E. adenocaulon'' and include those populations, while ''E. ciliatum'' ssp. ''glandulosum'' would perhaps use the name ''E. bergianum'' and include those populations. The others named  ''E. ciliatum'' ssp. ''ciliatum'' populations would remain.

==Distribution and habitat==
''Epilobium ciliatum'' is native to the southern part of Canada and most of the United States of America. It is a plant of moist places, stream-sides, ditches, ponds, gardens, roadsides, recently cleared areas and wasteland.<ref name=NatureGate/>

===Invasiveness===
It arrived in northern Europe early in the 20th century and spread rapidly, reaching Finland in about 1920.<ref name=NatureGate/> It reached Slovenia by 1993 and [[Zagorje]], Croatia by 2001. In Europe, ''Epilobium ciliatum'' competes with and is often found together with ''[[Epilobium roseum]]'', which prefers a similar habitat.{{sfn|Strgulc Krajšek|Šegedin|Jogan|2009|p=164}}
